A magnetic dipole oscillating in a field is a torsional pendulum with period
**2π√(I/mB)**.
**Step 1 — state the formula.**
T = 2π√(I/mB) ✓
with I the moment of inertia, m the magnetic moment and B the field.
**Step 2 — evaluate the bracket.**
mB = (6 x 10⁻²)(2 x 10⁻²) = **1·2 x 10⁻³**
I/mB = (12 x 10⁻⁶)/(1·2 x 10⁻³)
= **1 x 10⁻²** ✓
**Step 3 — find the period.**
T = 2π√(10⁻²)
= 2π(0·1)
= 0·2π
= **0·6 s** with π ≈ 3 ✓
**Step 4 — find the time for 20 oscillations.**
20 x 0·6 = **12 s** ✓
**Where the formula comes from.** The restoring torque on a dipole at angle θ to the
field is
τ = −mB sin θ ≈ **−mBθ** for small θ ✓
so Iθ̈ = −mBθ, which is simple harmonic with ω² = mB/I - exactly the structure of a
pendulum, with mB playing the part of the restoring constant.
**Why the oscillation must be small.** The approximation sin θ ≈ θ fails for large
swings ✓ at 30° the error is already 1·7%, and the motion is then not quite
sinusoidal.
**Why π ≈ 3 is given.** It makes 2π(0·1) = 0·6 exactly ✓ With the true π the period is
0·628 s and 20 oscillations take **12·6 s** - still nearest 12 s, so the approximation
does not change the answer.
**How such an experiment is used.** Timing the oscillations of a magnet in a field is
the standard way to measure **B**, or - with B known - the magnet's moment ✓ It is the
principle of the vibration magnetometer, used to measure the Earth's horizontal field.
**The analogy worth noting.**
simple pendulum: T = 2π√(l/g) ✓
torsional: T = 2π√(I/c)
magnetic dipole: T = 2π√(I/mB) ✓
all the same structure - inertia over restoring constant.
**A check on the units.**
[I/mB] = (kg m²)/[(A m²)(T)] = (kg m²)/(kg s⁻²) = **s²** ✓ so its square root is a
time.
**Reading the distractors.** **6 s** ✗ is ten oscillations. **36 s** ✗ is sixty, and
**18 s** ✗ thirty ✓ The period itself is 0·6 s, and the only arithmetic left is
multiplying by 20.
∴ 12 s.

Work out each dimensional formula and match it.
**Step 1 — torque.** Force x distance:
[τ] = [M L T⁻²][L] = **[M L² T⁻²]** → **(iv)** ✓
**Step 2 — gravitational constant.** From F = Gm₁m₂/r²:
[G] = [M L T⁻²][L²]/[M²] = **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]** → **(iii)** ✓
**Step 3 — capacitance.** From C = Q/V, with [V] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]:
[C] = [A T]/[M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹] = **[M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]** → **(i)** ✓
**Step 4 — Planck's constant.** From E = hν:
[h] = [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = **[M L² T⁻¹]** → **(ii)** ✓
**Step 5 — assemble.** a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii ✓
**The quickest way through such a question.** Look for the **distinctive** entry
first ✓ Only **capacitance** involves electric current, so (i) - the sole formula with
A in it - must be c. That alone eliminates two of the four codes.
**The next discriminator.** Only **G** has a **negative** power of mass among the
remaining three, so b must be (iii) ✓ The question is then settled without checking a
or d.
**Torque and work, a caution.** Both have dimensions [M L² T⁻²] ✓ They are quite
different physically - one a vector, one a scalar - but dimensionally identical, which
is why dimensional analysis cannot distinguish them.
**Planck's constant and angular momentum.** Also dimensionally identical,
[M L² T⁻¹] ✓ and here the identity **is** physically meaningful: h is the quantum of
angular momentum.
**A check on capacitance by another route.** C = ε₀A/d, and
[ε₀] = [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²], so
[C] = [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²][L²]/[L] = **[M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]** ✓ consistent.
**The units, as a cross-check.**
torque: **N m** ✓
G: **N m² kg⁻²** ✓
capacitance: **farad = C V⁻¹** ✓
h: **J s** ✓
Each reproduces its dimensional formula at once.
∴ a − iv, b − iii, c − i, d − ii.

Angular momentum is conserved when the **net external torque is zero**.
**Step 1 — state the rotational form of Newton's second law.**
**τ_ext = dL̄/dt** ✓
**Step 2 — set the torque to zero.**
dL̄/dt = 0, so **L̄ = constant** ✓
Angular momentum is conserved - in magnitude **and** direction.
**Step 3 — note what does not matter.** A net **force** can act without affecting
angular momentum, provided it exerts no **torque** about the chosen axis ✓ A force
directed through the axis has zero moment arm.
**The classic illustration - a central force.** A planet orbiting the Sun feels an
enormous force, but it is always directed **at** the Sun ✓ so the torque about the Sun
is zero and the planet's angular momentum is constant. That is exactly **Kepler's
second law**, equal areas in equal times.
**The skater.** Pulling her arms in reduces her moment of inertia, and with L = Iω
fixed her **angular velocity rises** ✓ No external torque acts - the forces are
internal - so L cannot change.
**Why the question's third option is wrong.** "Net external torque **is** applied" ✗
would make dL/dt non-zero and L change ✓ It is the exact negation of the answer.
**Why "net external force is applied" is not the criterion.** ✗ Force governs
**linear** momentum; torque governs **angular** ✓ A tangential force changes both; a
radial one changes only the linear momentum.
**Why "net pressure" is meaningless here.** ✗ Pressure is force per unit area and
appears nowhere in rotational dynamics ✓
**The three great conservation laws, side by side.**
no external **force** → **linear momentum** conserved ✓
no external **torque** → **angular momentum** conserved ✓
no non-conservative force → **mechanical energy** conserved ✓
**Why "external" matters.** Internal torques occur in equal and opposite pairs and
cancel ✓ An exploding shell, a collapsing star, a diver tucking - all redistribute
angular momentum internally without changing the total.
**Where it is most dramatic.** A collapsing star's radius falls by a factor of 10⁵, so
I falls by 10¹⁰ and ω rises by the same factor ✓ producing a **pulsar** spinning
hundreds of times a second.
∴ net external torque is not applied.

In a **uniform** field a dipole feels a torque and has a potential energy, but **no net
force**.
**Step 1 — check Statement I.** The torque on a dipole is
**τ̄ = P̄ x Ē** ✓ **correct**
Its magnitude is PE sin θ, greatest when the dipole is perpendicular to the field and
zero when aligned.
**Step 2 — check Statement II.** The potential energy is
**U = −P̄·Ē** ✓ **correct**
= −PE cos θ, lowest (−PE) when **aligned** with the field and highest (+PE) when
antiparallel - which is why a dipole tends to turn into alignment.
**Step 3 — check Statement III.** The forces on the two charges are **+qĒ** and
**−qĒ** ✓ equal and opposite, since the field is the **same** at both ends. They sum to
**zero**:
**F_net = 0** ✗ so Statement III is **wrong**.
**Step 4 — conclude.** **I and II only** ✓
**Why the two forces form a couple.** Equal, opposite and acting along **different**
lines ✓ A couple produces a **pure torque** with no resultant force - so the dipole
**rotates** but its centre of mass does not accelerate.
**What changes in a non-uniform field.** The forces on the two charges are then
**unequal**, and a net force survives ✓
F = P(dE/dx) for a dipole aligned along the gradient
This is why a charged comb attracts neutral paper: it polarises the paper and then pulls
the induced dipole towards the stronger field.
**The equilibrium positions.**
θ = 0: U = **−PE**, a **stable** minimum ✓
θ = 180°: U = **+PE**, an **unstable** maximum ✓
θ = 90°: U = **0**, and the torque is at its **greatest**
**The work to rotate the dipole.**
W = PE(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂) ✓ so turning it from aligned to antiparallel costs **2PE**.
**The magnetic analogue.** Exactly parallel: τ̄ = m̄ x B̄ and U = −m̄·B̄ ✓ A compass
needle in the Earth's uniform field turns but is not dragged along - the same physics.
**Reading the distractors.** Any option including **III** ✗ claims a net force in a
uniform field ✓ which the equal and opposite forces forbid.
∴ I and II only.

Conduction rate goes as **A/L**, with the area set by the **square** of the diameter.
**Step 1 — write the law of conduction.**
dQ/dt = **kA ΔT/L** ✓
With the same material and the same temperature difference, only A/L differs.
**Step 2 — find the area ratio.** A ∝ d², and the diameters are in the ratio 1 : 2:
A₁ : A₂ = **1 : 4** ✓
**Step 3 — note the length ratio.**
L₁ : L₂ = **2 : 1** ✓
**Step 4 — combine.**
(dQ/dt)₁ : (dQ/dt)₂ = (A₁/L₁) : (A₂/L₂)
= (1/2) : (4/1)
= 0·5 : 4
= **1 : 8** ✓
**Why the second conductor wins so decisively.** It is **four times** thicker in
cross-section **and** half as long ✓ Both help, and the effects multiply: 4 x 2 = **8**.
**Why the diameter counts twice over.** The area goes as d², so doubling the diameter
**quadruples** it ✓ Overlooking the square - and taking the area ratio as 1 : 2 - gives
1 : 4, which is the fourth distractor.
**The thermal-resistance view.** Define R_th = L/(kA) ✓ Then
dQ/dt = ΔT/R_th
exactly like Ohm's law, with temperature difference as the "voltage" and heat flow as
the "current". The first conductor has eight times the thermal resistance.
**A worked instance.** Take k = 400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (copper), ΔT = 100 K, d₁ = 1 mm,
L₁ = 2 m:
first: A = 7·85 x 10⁻⁷ m², dQ/dt = **0·0157 W**
second: d = 2 mm, L = 1 m, A = 3·14 x 10⁻⁶, dQ/dt = **0·126 W** ✓
ratio **1 : 8** ✓
**Why this matters practically.** Heat sinks are made short and broad; insulating
layers long and thin ✓ The same reasoning governs electrical conductors, where
R = ρL/A has the identical form.
**The steady-state assumption.** The formula applies once the temperature profile has
settled ✓ Before that the specific heat matters too, and the problem becomes a
differential equation.
**Reading the distractors.** **8 : 1** ✗ inverts the ratio - the **thinner, longer**
conductor must carry **less** heat. **4 : 1** and **1 : 4** ✗ account for the area but
not the length ✓
∴ 1 : 8.

Emission depends on the **wavelength**, never on the **power** of the lamp.
**Step 1 — state the threshold condition.** Photoelectrons are emitted only if
λ **<** λ₀ = **5200 Å** ✓
equivalently ν > ν₀, or hν > the work function.
**Step 2 — place the options on the spectrum.**
**infrared**: λ > 7000 Å ✓ **longer** than the threshold, so **no** emission - whatever
the lamp's power
**ultraviolet**: λ < 4000 Å ✓ **shorter** than the threshold, so emission occurs
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the **50 W UV lamp** ejects electrons ✓
**Why the wattage is irrelevant to whether emission occurs.** Light arrives as
**photons**, and each electron absorbs **one** ✓ A photon of infrared simply does not
carry enough energy, and a million of them do not help - no electron can accumulate
energy from several.
**What the power does control.** The **number** of photoelectrons, and hence the
**current** ✓ A brighter UV lamp gives more electrons, each with the same maximum
kinetic energy.
**Why three IR lamps of different powers are offered.** To test exactly this point ✓
50 W, 10 W and 1 W of infrared all give the same result: **nothing**. The 50 W UV lamp
and the 50 W IR lamp have identical power, and only one works.
**The work function here.**
φ = hc/λ₀ = 1240/520 = **2·38 eV** ✓ typical of a sensitive photo-emissive surface such
as caesium-antimony.
**The energies compared.**
infrared at 10000 Å: **1·24 eV** - well below threshold ✗
threshold at 5200 Å: **2·38 eV** ✓
ultraviolet at 3000 Å: **4·13 eV** - comfortably above ✓ giving photoelectrons with up
to 1·75 eV of kinetic energy.
**Why classical wave theory failed here.** It predicted that **any** frequency would
work given enough intensity or time ✓ The existence of a sharp threshold, and the
instantaneous emission above it, could only be explained by Einstein's photon
hypothesis of 1905 - for which he received the Nobel Prize.
**Reading the distractors.** All three **IR** options ✗ fail on wavelength, and their
differing powers are precisely the distraction ✓
∴ 50 W UV lamp.

A **good absorber is a good emitter** - so the blue glass, which absorbs red, glows red
most strongly when hot.
**Step 1 — see why the glass looks blue.** It **transmits** blue and **absorbs** red ✓
That selective absorption is what gives it its colour.
**Step 2 — apply Kirchhoff's law of radiation.** At a given wavelength and temperature,
**emissivity = absorptivity** ✓ A body that absorbs strongly at some wavelength must
also **emit** strongly there.
**Step 3 — heat the blue glass.** Being a strong absorber of **red**, it is a strong
**emitter** of red ✓ So at high temperature it radiates vigorously in the red.
**Step 4 — compare with the red glass.** That piece **transmits** red and absorbs blue,
so it is a **poor** emitter of red ✓ and in any case it is only at room temperature.
**Step 5 — conclude.** The blue piece **shines like a brighter red** than the red
piece ✓
**Why Kirchhoff's law must hold.** Consider a body in an enclosure at the same
temperature ✓ If it absorbed more than it emitted at some wavelength it would heat up
spontaneously, violating the second law. Absorptivity and emissivity must therefore be
equal at every wavelength.
**The classic demonstration.** Paint a white pattern on a piece of china and heat it
in a furnace ✓ Viewed in the dark, the pattern appears **dark** against a bright
background - the white regions, being poor absorbers, are poor emitters. The image is
**reversed**.
**Another familiar case.** The **sodium** vapour in the Sun's atmosphere absorbs the
yellow D lines, producing dark Fraunhofer lines ✓ Heated in a flame, the same vapour
**emits** at exactly those wavelengths.
**Why the blue glass does not look blue when hot.** Its own thermal emission in the red
far outweighs any blue it transmits in a dimly lit room ✓ The colour we see is now
emitted, not transmitted.
**The ideal limiting case.** A **perfect black body** absorbs everything and therefore
emits the maximum possible at every wavelength ✓ Its spectrum is Planck's law, and no
real body can exceed it.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Blue looks blue, red as usual**" ✗ ignores the glass's
own emission. "**Red looks brighter**" ✗ reverses the roles - the red glass is the poor
emitter of red ✓
∴ blue shines like brighter red compared to the red piece.
